title: Hashes, defaults, and grouped totals
summary: Total order rows with a default-zero hash, then diagnose a shared default array that leaks items across categories.

objectives.description: Accumulate rows into a default-zero hash.
Find the shared mutable default behind duplicate items.
Choose a safe default for grouping lists.

hints: rows.each_with_object starts from a hash you control.
Hash.new(0) gives a missing key a numeric default.
The block receives each row and the accumulating hash.
Add row[:amount] to the category total.

misconceptions.description: Switching to nil and appending without creating a list.
misconceptions.feedback: Hash.new(nil) still returns nothing to append to. The block default must create and store a new array for each key.

misconceptions.description: Adding to a missing key that defaults to nil.
misconceptions.testDescription: Each category accumulates into a default-zero hash.
misconceptions.feedback: A plain hash returns nil for a missing key, and nil + amount raises NoMethodError. Supply a zero default or fetch with a fallback.

misconceptions.description: Using a mutable string default for grouped names.
misconceptions.feedback: Hash.new("") shares one string object. Use a block such as Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] } so each key gets its own value.

misconceptions.description: Reading string keys from rows that use symbols.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Looking up row["category"] when the rows store row[:category].
misconceptions.feedback: A Ruby symbol is not a string. Read the same key type the producer wrote, or normalize keys at the boundary.

sections.title: Hashes map keys to values
sections.body: A Hash stores key-value pairs: { tools: 5, paper: 2 }. A missing key returns nil by default. Ruby distinguishes symbol keys from string keys, so row[:category] and row["category"] are different lookups. Use symbols for fixed field names and normalize external input at the boundary.

sections.title: Defaults can be shared
sections.body: Hash.new(0) returns the same immutable zero for every missing key, so totals[key] += amount works: the read returns zero, then assignment stores the sum. Hash.new([]) is different: every missing key returns the same mutable array object. Appending to it mutates one array that all those keys share. Use Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] } to create a fresh array per key.

sections.title: each_with_object keeps state local
sections.body: rows.each_with_object(Hash.new(0)) do |row, totals| ... end passes the same accumulator into each block and returns it at the end. The block's return value is ignored, so no separate assignment is needed. Prefer this over a method-level mutable hash when a helper may be called concurrently or reused.

An iteration that threads an explicit accumulator through a block.
An immutable name such as :tools used as a hash key.
One mutable object returned for every missing key, causing cross-key mutation.

steps.title: Every category shows every item
steps.prompt: The grouped report lists the same items under unrelated categories. Select the faulty instruction and the correct repair.
hints: The bug appears only when a key is read before it is stored.
Hash.new takes one default object, not a factory.
An array default is mutable and shared.
Use a block default that stores a new array per key.

fixes.label: Call .dup on the list after every insert.

steps.explanation: Hash.new([]) evaluates the array once, so every missing key returns the same object. A block default runs per key and stores a fresh array, keeping categories independent.

steps.title: Pick a safe grouping default
steps.prompt: The next report groups item names by category. Which hash construction keeps each category's list independent?
hints: The default must create a new list for each missing key.
A plain object argument is evaluated once.
A block default runs on each miss.
Store the new list inside the block.

quiz.prompt: The next report groups item names by category. Which hash construction keeps each category's list independent?
quiz.explanation: The block runs for each missing key and stores a new array. Hash.new([]) and Hash.new("") share one mutable object, and nil cannot be appended to.
